paragraphs: The Rasch model describes binary responses, such as answering a question correctly or liking a movie, through the difference between a user parameter and an item parameter. This paper develops a new way to estimate the item parameters. The task matters because those parameters help characterize items across settings ranging from educational testing to recommendation.

The algorithm builds a graph connecting items and defines a Markov chain on that graph. Its central computation finds the chain’s stationary distribution: the long-run distribution of probability across items. This turns item estimation into a spectral problem, providing a different computational route for fitting this established response model.

The authors provide finite-sample error guarantees, establish consistency, and show favorable optimality properties. They also discuss practical changes that improve speed and robustness. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets, including small testing datasets and large recommendation datasets, report scalable, accurate performance competitive with commonly used methods. Together, the theory and experiments support the approach as a practical estimation alternative.
neurips-2022-a-spectral-approach-to-item.tldr: A graph-based spectral algorithm estimates Rasch item parameters with finite-sample guarantees and competitive empirical accuracy and scalability.

paragraphs: Transformers can connect information across distant image patches, which helps object detectors understand broad visual context. The paper argues that these models can still leave useful local detail insufficiently explored. CFDT addresses this gap by connecting coarse representations of the image with finer representations that preserve more localized information.

The detector introduces three components with complementary roles. A local-global cross fusion module connects fine local features and coarse global features. A coarse-fine aware neck allows detection tokens to interact with both kinds of representation. An additional feature integration module combines representations at multiple scales from different processing stages, bringing these sources of information together efficiently.

On COCO, the authors report 48.1 AP at 173G FLOPs. In their comparison, CFDT achieves higher accuracy with less computation than the transformer detector ViDT. These results support the proposed combination of global context, local detail, and information across scales. The contribution is an architecture that makes these representations interact throughout detection, with an empirical improvement in the reported accuracy and computation tradeoff.
neurips-2022-a-transformer-based-object-.tldr: CFDT connects coarse global context with fine local features to improve the reported accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based object detection.

paragraphs: ASPiRe studies how reinforcement learning can reuse earlier experience when learning a new task. It learns a library of specialized behavior priors from separate datasets. Keeping these priors distinct gives the learner multiple sources of behavioral guidance, with the aim of making the acquired experience more reusable across downstream tasks.

The main challenge is deciding which priors are useful and how they should work together. A new task may require behaviors in sequence or in combination. ASPiRe introduces an Adaptive Weight Module that learns how much weight to assign to different priors. These weights guide policy learning through weighted Kullback-Leibler divergences, which measure differences between the learned policy and the prior behaviors.

The experiments show that ASPiRe can substantially accelerate downstream learning when multiple priors are available and improve over competitive baselines. The findings support adaptive combination as a useful part of experience reuse: having several specialized priors creates an opportunity, while learning their relative influence helps turn that collection into guidance for a new task.
neurips-2022-aspire-adaptive-skill-prior.tldr: ASPiRe accelerates reinforcement learning by learning how to combine specialized behavior priors for new tasks.

paragraphs: Partial AUC evaluates a binary classifier within selected false-positive or true-positive rate ranges. This makes it useful when performance must satisfy particular decision constraints. The paper addresses a difficulty in optimizing this measure: existing approximations can introduce uncontrolled bias, while an unbiased formulation based on pairs of examples has scalability and convergence drawbacks.

The authors reformulate both one-way and two-way partial AUC using functions of individual examples. Their formulation is asymptotically unbiased and produces a regularized min-max problem that is nonconvex in one part and strongly concave in the other. Working with individual examples gives the proposed solver computational cost per iteration that grows linearly with sample size.

The paper also supplies a time-complexity guarantee for reaching an approximate stationary point. The same reformulation makes generalization analysis easier and yields error bounds that accommodate real-valued model outputs. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines a more scalable optimization formulation with theoretical control over optimization and generalization, while retaining the qualification that unbiasedness is asymptotic.
neurips-2022-asymptotically-unbiased-ins.tldr: An asymptotically unbiased, instance-wise partial-AUC formulation improves optimization scalability and simplifies generalization analysis.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to adapt an existing probabilistic classifier to satisfy specified group-fairness requirements when there are multiple possible classes. The starting classifier may be unfair. The proposed approach frames the correction as a projection onto the set of classifiers that meet the chosen requirements, making those requirements part of the mathematical construction.

The resulting classifier is obtained by post-processing the original model’s outputs with a multiplicative factor. To compute this adjustment, the authors develop an iterative algorithm that can run in parallel. They also derive sample-complexity and convergence guarantees, providing theoretical support for both the data requirements and the procedure used to obtain the projected classifier.

Numerical comparisons show competitive tradeoffs between accuracy and fairness, alongside favorable runtime on large datasets. The method is also evaluated on an open dataset containing more than one million samples, multiple classes, and multiple intersectional groups. This broader evaluation supports its practical relevance to fairness settings involving several overlapping groups and more than two prediction outcomes.
neurips-2022-beyond-adult-and-compas-fai.tldr: A parallelizable post-processing method adjusts multiclass prediction probabilities to meet target group-fairness requirements with competitive accuracy-fairness tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often describe a node’s surroundings by gathering information from nearby nodes. Random walks offer one way to encode these structures, and their probability distributions evolve through diffusion governed by the graph Laplacian. This paper extends that mathematical starting point to develop a richer operator for representing graph structure.

Using results about hypo-elliptic diffusions, the authors introduce a tensor-valued operator called the hypo-elliptic graph Laplacian. They supply theoretical guarantees and efficient low-rank approximation algorithms. The resulting construction offers a structured way to capture dependencies across distant parts of a graph while remaining robust to pooling, an operation that combines graph information into a coarser representation.

Experiments show performance competitive with graph transformers on datasets that require long-range reasoning. The reported scaling is linear in the number of edges, compared with quadratic scaling in the number of nodes for the graph-transformer comparison. This combination matters because it links a mathematically structured representation of distant relationships with a computational cost tied to graph connectivity.
neurips-2022-capturing-graphs-with-hypo-.tldr: A tensor-valued diffusion operator captures long-range graph relationships with competitive empirical performance and computation that scales linearly with edges.

paragraphs: Error-correction decoding recovers transmitted information after a communication channel introduces noise. Neural decoders have shown strong results, but the paper identifies two difficulties in existing approaches: overfitting associated with exponential training complexity and restrictive assumptions inherited from belief propagation. It proposes a transformer architecture for soft decoding of linear codes at arbitrary block lengths.

Each dimension of the channel output is embedded into a higher-dimensional representation, allowing the model to process information about individual bits separately. This element-wise processing supports assessment of the reliability of received information. An adapted masked self-attention module incorporates the algebraic structure of the code and interactions between bits.

The design gives separate roles to local reliability information and code-dependent relationships, while using attention to combine them during decoding. The authors report large improvements over existing state-of-the-art neural decoders at a fraction of their time complexity. These findings support transformers as a flexible architecture for this decoding problem, with the reported gains covering both decoding performance and computational demands.
neurips-2022-error-correction-code-trans.tldr: A transformer decoder combines bit-reliability representations with code-aware masked attention and reports substantial gains over existing neural decoders.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether protection against adversarial perturbations also helps when data changes naturally between training and deployment. It shows that these forms of robustness can conflict. The theoretical analysis starts with linear regression on Gaussian data, separating core features from spurious features whose training correlations may change in a new domain.

Within that setting, adversarial training using ℓ1 or ℓ2 norms increases reliance on spurious features. For ℓ∞ training, this reliance occurs only when spurious features have larger scale than core features. If their correlations change at test time, adversarial training can consequently reduce robustness to the new distribution. These conclusions retain specific dependencies on the training norm and feature setting.

Experiments with twenty adversarially trained models across five datasets find greater reliance on backgrounds than in standardly trained counterparts. The authors also show that spurious correlations can improve adversarial robustness when those correlations persist at test time. The findings challenge a simple association between spurious features and adversarial vulnerability, showing why the type of robustness and the behavior of correlations both matter.
neurips-2022-explicit-tradeoffs-between-.tldr: Theory and experiments show that adversarial training can increase spurious-feature reliance and weaken robustness when those correlations change.

paragraphs: Length generalization is the ability to learn from shorter problems and handle longer ones. It matters when long training examples are scarce, as can happen in mathematical reasoning, theorem proving, and work with long texts. This paper empirically investigates how transformer language models perform when the length of a problem extends beyond their learning examples.

The authors first find substantial weaknesses when transformers are naively finetuned for length-generalization tasks. Increasing model scale does not remove these deficiencies in the studied setting. They then combine pretrained models’ ability to learn from examples in context with scratchpad prompting, which asks for intermediate solution steps before the final answer.

That combination produces a dramatic improvement in the reported length-generalization results. The paper also analyzes failures across the different learning approaches and identifies recurring sources of mistakes. These findings make the learning setup and prompting procedure central to the discussion: the study reports meaningful improvement through their combination, while its failure analysis shows that generalizing to longer problems still presents unresolved challenges.
neurips-2022-exploring-length-generaliza.tldr: Combining in-context learning with scratchpad prompting substantially improves length generalization where naive transformer finetuning shows persistent weaknesses.

paragraphs: Many successful near-neighbor search methods find relevant items by walking through a graph that links nearby items. Even when this search strategy works well, its memory accesses can be inefficient. The paper measures poor cache behavior in popular indices such as HNSW, identifying memory layout as an opportunity to accelerate queries.

The authors formulate graph traversal as a task of maximizing cache hits. They apply graph reordering, which places nodes that are commonly accessed together near one another in memory. They also mathematically connect the graph’s layout to the cache complexity of search, explaining why the arrangement of stored nodes affects the cost of following graph connections.

Experiments apply several reordering algorithms to an HNSW-based search method. The reported query-time improvement reaches up to 40%, while reordering takes negligible time compared with constructing the index. The paper also analyzes and improves existing layout methods. These findings show that organizing an index’s memory layout can deliver substantial practical speedups alongside the choices made in the search algorithm itself.
neurips-2022-graph-reordering-for-cache-.tldr: Reordering graph nodes to improve cache locality reduces HNSW query time by up to 40% in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search studies how to choose a network’s structure, but training hyperparameters can be at least as consequential in some settings. This motivates joint architecture and hyperparameter search, where the two are explored together. JAHS-Bench-201 provides surrogate benchmarks intended to make research on this expensive combined search problem more accessible.

The collection extends the NAS-Bench-201 space to a 14-dimensional search and fidelity space. It is built from approximately 161 million data points covering twenty performance metrics across three deep learning tasks. Its design also supports research that considers multiple objectives, computational cost, and evaluations at different fidelity levels.

The practical aim is to let researchers evaluate search algorithms with far less computation through surrogate evaluations of network performance. The authors give an example of reducing an algorithm run from five days to a few seconds. This makes the benchmark useful as shared infrastructure for investigating how architecture choices and hyperparameters interact, including settings where accuracy must be considered alongside other objectives or evaluation costs.
neurips-2022-jahs-bench-201-a-foundation.tldr: JAHS-Bench-201 supplies large-scale surrogate benchmarks to make joint architecture and hyperparameter search research much less computationally expensive.

paragraphs: Online covering optimization requires an algorithm to respond as constraints arrive. For semidefinite programs, known impossibility results restrict how closely online methods can approximate the optimal solution. This paper studies what becomes possible when the algorithm also receives advice from a predictor that may sometimes be wrong.

The proposed framework aims for two guarantees. With accurate predictions, it achieves a constant-factor approximation, a property called consistency. With inaccurate predictions, it matches classical optimal bounds up to constant factors under stated technical conditions, providing robustness. Accurate advice supplies additional information that allows the method to bypass the impossibility results of the original online setting.

The authors develop general algorithms for covering linear programs with fractional advice and constraints, and extend learning-augmented optimization to covering semidefinite programs. Their techniques use a primal-dual framework and can be adjusted for box constraints that restrict variables to bounded regions. The contribution is a way to benefit from reliable predictions while retaining conditional worst-case protection when advice is poor.
neurips-2022-learning-augmented-algorith.tldr: Prediction-augmented online covering algorithms achieve constant-factor guarantees with accurate advice and retain classical robustness bounds under technical conditions.

paragraphs: Forecasting a time series is difficult when several kinds of variation are entangled. Recurring seasonal behavior and broader trends can overlap, making useful patterns hard to extract. LaST approaches this problem by learning separate latent representations intended to describe these two components, drawing on both classical time-series decomposition and disentangled representation learning.

The method uses variational inference to learn the seasonal and trend representations. It introduces auxiliary objectives that supervise the representations and encourage their separation. These objectives consider both the representations themselves and their role in reconstructing the input, connecting the desired separation to the observed time series.

The authors report state-of-the-art forecasting results in extensive experiments against advanced representation-learning methods and end-to-end forecasting models. The findings support the usefulness of explicitly organizing the learned representation around seasonality and trend. The central contribution is therefore a forecasting approach that gives these components separate roles in latent space and trains that separation through several complementary objectives, with empirical results supporting the overall design.
neurips-2022-learning-latent-seasonal-tr.tldr: LaST learns separate latent seasonal and trend representations and reports state-of-the-art time-series forecasting performance.

paragraphs: MEMO addresses models that encounter unfamiliar corruptions or other distribution shifts after training. It adapts a model using the test example itself, including settings where only one example is available. The method does not require a particular training procedure, but it does require a probabilistic model whose parameters can be adapted.

For a test example, MEMO creates several augmented versions and averages the model’s predicted distributions across them. It then updates all model parameters to minimize the entropy of this average distribution. This objective encourages confident predictions that agree across the augmentations, making the transformations used for augmentation a source of guidance during adaptation.

Across the evaluated ResNet and vision-transformer models, the authors report accuracy gains of 1–8% over standard evaluation and generally better results than prior augmentation and adaptation strategies. In the single-example setting, they report state-of-the-art results on ImageNet-C and ImageNet-R, and among ResNet-50 models on ImageNet-A. These findings support adapting to an individual input as a useful approach to robustness under the tested distribution shifts.
neurips-2022-memo-test-time-robustness-v.tldr: MEMO improves test-time robustness by adapting a model to make confident, consistent predictions across augmentations of a single input.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning seeks representations that preserve information shared across distorted versions of an input. This paper examines interference from irrelevant information and inefficient use of training examples. It connects these problems to redundancy across representation dimensions and to dimensions containing confounding information, providing experimental evidence for that interpretation.

MetaMask combines redundancy reduction with a learned mask over representation dimensions. The redundancy-reduction component addresses duplicated information, while the mask reduces the gradient effects of particular dimensions containing confounders. A meta-learning procedure trains the mask with the objective of improving the masked representation’s performance on a self-supervised task.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that MetaMask can obtain tighter downstream classification risk bounds than typical contrastive methods. They also report state-of-the-art results across various benchmarks. The approach matters because it changes how individual dimensions influence learning, alongside efforts to make dimensions less redundant. Its stated theoretical and empirical findings support treating the internal organization of a representation as a meaningful target for improving self-supervised learning.
neurips-2022-metamask-revisiting-dimensi.tldr: MetaMask uses redundancy reduction and a meta-learned dimensional mask to improve self-supervised representations and downstream classification risk bounds.

paragraphs: Neural differential equations describe neural computation through continuously evolving states. Learning rules can also be expressed in continuous time because many update a network through repeated additive changes. This paper combines these two ideas to build sequence-processing models that learn how to modify the rapidly changing connections of another network.

Those changing connections serve as short-term memory. The model learns to manipulate that memory through continuous learning rules, yielding continuous-time versions of Fast Weight Programmers and linear Transformers. This connects sequence processing with a form of learned programming: one network controls changes in the connections used by another network to process information.

On several time-series classification tasks, the proposed models outperform the best existing models based on Neural Controlled Differential Equations in the reported comparisons. The authors also state that the approach addresses fundamental scalability limitations of those models. The contribution therefore joins a new continuous-time memory mechanism with empirical classification improvements and a response to the computational scaling difficulties of the compared model family.
neurips-2022-neural-differential-equatio.tldr: Continuous learning rules let neural differential-equation models manipulate fast-changing connection weights as memory, improving reported time-series classification results.

paragraphs: A classifier may exploit misleading training correlations, such as backgrounds associated with particular objects. This paper asks how much useful information about the actual target remains in its learned representation. That question separates the quality of the learned features from the way the final prediction layer uses them.

The authors evaluate representations by retraining only the last layer on held-out data where the spurious correlation is broken, following Deep Feature Reweighting. Across several vision and language problems, ordinary empirical risk minimization learns features highly competitive with those from specialized group-robustness training. Architecture and pretraining choices strongly affect feature quality, while strong regularization is not necessary for learning high-quality representations.

Using these insights, the authors report improved worst-group accuracies of 97% on Waterbirds, 92% on CelebA hair-color prediction, and 50% on WILDS-FMOW. The results indicate that models trained conventionally can retain useful core information even when spurious correlations influence their predictions. They also highlight the importance of representation design and the held-out data used to reweight those features.
neurips-2022-on-feature-learning-in-the-.tldr: Standard training can learn core features competitive with specialized robustness methods, and retraining the final layer helps reveal their quality.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the accuracy of a Gaussian-noise mechanism for privately approximating a symmetric matrix with a matrix having prescribed eigenvalues. Accuracy is measured by Frobenius distance, which summarizes matrix-entry errors. The new bounds depend on the target eigenvalues and on gaps between eigenvalues of the original matrix.

The analysis treats adding Gaussian noise as a continuous-time matrix Brownian motion. This viewpoint makes it possible to track changes in eigenvalues and eigenvectors through stochastic differential equations associated with Dyson. It yields an error bound that combines eigenvector perturbations through a square root of summed squares, improving on an analysis that adds separate perturbation bounds.

The guarantees hold when the top k+1 eigenvalues have sufficiently large gaps. Under this condition, applying the bounds to private rank-k covariance approximation and subspace recovery improves previous guarantees. The contribution is a sharper analysis of the Gaussian mechanism that uses the matrix’s spectral structure, with the eigenvalue-separation requirement playing an explicit role in when the results apply.
neurips-2022-re-analyze-gauss-bounds-for.tldr: A Brownian-motion analysis sharpens private matrix-approximation error bounds when the leading eigenvalues are sufficiently separated.

paragraphs: Propose-Test-Release is a privacy framework built around local sensitivity, making it useful for releasing robust statistics such as medians and trimmed means. Applying it repeatedly in adaptive procedures, including robust gradient-based training, requires careful accounting of accumulated privacy loss. This paper addresses that challenge through Rényi differential privacy.

The authors generalize the standard framework and derive its first Rényi privacy bound. They show that this analysis yields tighter differential-privacy guarantees than direct analysis in the usual epsilon-delta form. They also derive a subsampling amplification bound tailored to the algorithm, reporting that it is much tighter than a general upper bound and close to the lower bound.

These results enable tighter accounting across many adaptive uses of Propose-Test-Release. As an application, the authors construct private versions of Byzantine-robust training methods that aggregate gradients with robust statistics. Experiments involving label, feature, and gradient corruption across datasets and architectures show significantly improved utility over the baseline. The theoretical accounting thus supports a practical combination of privacy protection and robustness to corrupted training information.
neurips-2022-renyi-differential-privacy-.tldr: New Rényi privacy bounds for Propose-Test-Release improve repeated-query accounting and support private, corruption-robust training with better reported utility.

paragraphs: LiDAR-based object detection becomes difficult when objects contain only a few observed points, as often happens for small, distant, or incomplete objects. Sparse2Dense addresses this by learning richer 3D features from ordinary sparse point clouds. Its aim is to bring information associated with dense inputs into the detector’s internal representation.

The framework first trains a detector using dense point clouds. A second detector receives regular point clouds and includes a lightweight S2D module and a point-cloud reconstruction module. During training, this sparse-input detector learns to produce features that follow the dense features of the first detector, using the dense-input model as a source of guidance.

At inference time, the sparse-input detector can simulate dense features without requiring dense point clouds. Evaluations on the Waymo Open Dataset and Waymo Domain Adaptation Dataset report strong performance and efficiency relative to state-of-the-art methods. The key practical contribution is this separation between training guidance and inference requirements: dense inputs help teach the representation, while ordinary sparse inputs suffice when the trained detector is used.
neurips-2022-sparse2dense-learning-to-de.tldr: Sparse2Dense teaches a sparse-input 3D detector to imitate dense features, improving reported detection performance without dense inputs at inference.

paragraphs: This paper studies why shallow neural networks trained with gradient methods can generalize beyond their training data. It uses algorithmic stability, which connects sensitivity to changes in training data with generalization behavior. The analysis covers both gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent, two common ways to update network parameters.

For both methods, the authors derive consistent excess-risk bounds by using early stopping to balance optimization progress against generalization. The stopping decision is therefore part of the theoretical guarantee. Compared with previous gradient-descent analysis, the new results require a weaker overparameterization assumption and extend the treatment to stochastic gradient descent.

The improvement comes from tracking the optimization iterates more precisely. That refined control gives better estimates of the smallest eigenvalues of Hessian matrices associated with the empirical risk and loss along the training trajectories. These curvature estimates strengthen the stability analysis. The result is a more permissive theoretical account of generalization for the shallow networks studied, explicitly connecting network size assumptions, training dynamics, and when training stops.
neurips-2022-stability-and-generalizatio.tldr: A refined stability analysis gives early-stopping generalization guarantees for shallow networks under a weaker overparameterization assumption.

paragraphs: A video can contain many objects and events, while a text query may describe only one part of it. Representing the entire video with a single feature creates a matching problem: that feature must correspond to several different descriptions. This paper calls the issue video-text correspondence ambiguity and addresses it with multiple visual prototypes.

The model adaptively aggregates video-token features into several prototype representations. For a given query, it uses the most similar prototype to determine the match, allowing different texts to connect with different represented aspects of the same video. A variance loss encourages the prototypes to attend to different content so that they collectively reflect more of the video’s information.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods on four public video-retrieval datasets. The approach matters because it builds the possibility of multiple valid descriptions directly into the video representation and matching procedure. Its empirical results support using diverse prototypes and query-dependent selection to handle videos whose contents cannot be adequately matched through one shared feature.
neurips-2022-text-adaptive-multiple-visu.tldr: Multiple visual prototypes let different text queries match different parts of a video, improving retrieval on four reported datasets.

paragraphs: Object detectors need confidence estimates that meaningfully reflect the reliability of their predictions, especially when the input domain changes. This paper studies that calibration problem for detection, extending attention beyond visual classification and predictions made within the training domain. It develops two methods that can also be used together.

The first is TCD, an auxiliary calibration loss applied during training. It is designed to work alongside application-specific detection losses and across different detector paradigms. The second is an implicit calibration technique for self-training-based domain adaptation, supported by a new mechanism for quantifying uncertainty in object detection.

Experiments show notable calibration improvements from TCD for both in-domain and out-of-domain predictions, as well as across several domain-adaptive detectors and challenging adaptation settings. Combining the implicit technique with TCD during adaptation produces further improvements in the studied scenarios. These findings support addressing calibration both through an explicit training objective and through the adaptation procedure, making confidence quality a deliberate part of detector training under domain shift.
neurips-2022-towards-improving-calibrati.tldr: An auxiliary training loss and an uncertainty-based adaptation technique improve object-detector calibration across reported domain shifts.

paragraphs: Universality results describe a network family’s ability to approximate functions. For group convolutional networks, earlier proofs often required separate constructions for different layers or indirect connections to other universal approximators. This paper develops a unified, constructive analysis for depth-two group convolutional networks that more directly explains how parameters represent functions.

The authors formulate a continuous network as a mapping between group representations. They derive a ridgelet transform that maps a target function to network parameters, with the resulting continuous network representing that function. The construction covers examples including cyclic convolution on multichannel images, Deep Sets, and networks equivariant to Euclidean transformations.

Discretizing the closed-form transform yields constructive proofs of cc-universality for finite networks. This connects an explicit continuous representation with finite-network approximation guarantees. The significance lies in the description of how parameters are organized to represent a function, alongside the unification of several network types within one analysis. The authors identify this as the first ridgelet-transform construction for group convolutional neural networks.
neurips-2022-universality-of-group-convo.tldr: A ridgelet transform provides an explicit, unified route from target functions to universality proofs for depth-two group convolutional networks.

paragraphs: ViTPose investigates how well a plain vision transformer can estimate human pose. Its architecture uses a non-hierarchical transformer to extract features for a person instance, followed by a lightweight decoder that predicts pose. The study examines this simple structure through scalability, training flexibility, and transfer of knowledge between models.

The model family scales from 100 million to one billion parameters, with the authors reporting a new Pareto frontier between throughput and performance. ViTPose also accommodates different attention types, input resolutions, pretraining and finetuning strategies, and multiple pose tasks. Experiments further show that a simple knowledge token can transfer knowledge from large ViTPose models to smaller ones.

On the MS COCO Keypoint Detection benchmark, the basic model outperforms representative methods, while the largest establishes a new state of the art. These results support plain transformers as strong pose-estimation backbones. The contribution combines evidence for a straightforward architecture with an exploration of how that architecture can scale, adapt to training choices, and pass knowledge to smaller models.
neurips-2022-vitpose-simple-vision-trans.tldr: ViTPose shows that plain vision transformers with lightweight decoders can deliver scalable, flexible, state-of-the-art human pose estimation.
